meta.title: Serbian A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Serbian → English (see the Serbian, recall the meaning) and English → Serbian (see an English meaning, recall the Serbian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded Serbian word list could be used, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 363 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, people and family, numbers, telling the time, days, months and seasons, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, everyday verbs, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 137 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Serbian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The Serbian is the standard of Serbia: Ekavian (млеко, време, леп, not the Ijekavian млијеко, вријеме, лијеп of Bosnia and Montenegro), and words Wiktionary marks as only Croatian or Bosnian are left out. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic, the official alphabet, with its accent marked as Wiktionary gives it (ку̏ћа, вре́ме), and again in the Latin alphabet beneath (kuća, vreme), since Serbian is read in both every day; the Serbian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters, the two alphabets and the accent marks. The 182 nouns show their gender, their genitive and their plural; the 107 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, their ја and он forms and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's seven cases and every verb's present, future, past and imperative. Real example sentences come with 482 of the 500 words, three apiece for 457 of them, in Cyrillic with the Latin spelling beneath, the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, accents and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
